title: Cluster randomised controlled trial in general practice with an extended health economic evaluation to assess the efficacy and health-economic impact of hypertonic saline nasal spray for respiratory tract infections
summary:
Respiratory tract infections (like colds and sore throats) are very common and can be a real burden – not just for the people who get sick, but also for doctors, hospitals, and health systems. This study is asking a simple but important question: Can using a hypertonic nasal spray early on help adults recover faster and feel better?
The spray being tested is a hypertonic saline spray (about 3% salt), which is safe, easy to use, and available without a prescription. Researchers want to know if using it regularly at the first sign of a cold or respiratory infection can:

    Shorten how long the illness lasts,
    Make symptoms less severe,
    Help people stay at work or keep up with daily activities,
    Reduce the need for medicines – especially antibiotics,
    And improve overall well-being and quality of life.

The study is also looking at the cost side: Will using this spray save money for health insurance and society? Is it worth the cost? Could it reduce doctor visits, sick days, or unnecessary antibiotic use?
This is the first large-scale study of its kind in Germany, carried out directly in general practitioner (GP) offices – so it’s based on real-life medical care, not just a hospital setting.
To make sure everything runs smoothly, the researchers will also check how well the study works in practice – asking patients, doctors, and study staff what they thought about the process, what worked well, and what could be improved.
How does the study work?
A total of 200 GP clinics across Germany will be randomly assigned to one of three groups:

    Group 1: Use the nasal spray six times a day (two sprays in each nostril) – in addition to usual care.
    Group 2: Use the spray twice a day – again, plus usual care.
    Group 3: Receive only usual care – no extra spray.

The study aims to include 3,840 adults who are healthy at the start (no active cold or infection) and will be followed for one full year. Participants must have had at least two respiratory infections in the past year, or be at higher risk of complications (like older adults or people with other health conditions).
People will be recruited at the start of two winter seasons – because that’s when colds and infections are most common.
What will they measure?
Researchers will compare how quickly people recover, how bad their symptoms are, how many days they miss work, how many medications they take, and how they feel about their health.
To make sure the results are reliable, they’ll also look at other factors that might affect outcomes – like age, income, mental health, stress levels, or other illnesses.
They’ll also check how well people stick to the treatment – do they actually use the spray as instructed?
Finally, they’ll do a full cost analysis from the perspective of Germany’s public health insurance system – to see if the spray is cost-effective and could lead to real savings.
In short:
This study is testing whether a simple, safe, and cheap nasal spray – used early in a cold – can help people feel better faster, stay productive, and reduce pressure on the healthcare system. It’s one of the biggest real-world tests of its kind in Germany, and could show that something as simple as a saltwater spray might make a big difference in everyday health.

interventions.name: use of hypertonic saline nasal spray (two sprays per nostril six times per day until symptoms are resolved) in addition to usual care upon the onset of the first RTI-symptoms over the 12-month observation period

use of hypertonic saline nasal spray (two sprays per nostril two times per day until symptoms are resolved) in addition to usual care upon the onset of the first RTI-symptoms over the 12-month observation period
Control: usual care (as advised) when RTI-symptoms occur, over the 12-month observation period

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1) with a history of at least two RTIs in the past 12 months 
 or 
2) who are at increased risk of adverse outcomes from RTI, based on the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Vaccination for the standard vaccination against RTI pathogens. The latter include risk factors such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular, liver and kidney diseases, obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), age >60, disease- or drug-induced immunodeficiency etc.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients with severe physical illness (e.g. advanced cancer, severe heart disease), severe mental illness (e.g. dementia, schizophrenia), hyperaldosteronism, significant mobility impairment, those in palliative care or nursing home residents, as well as individuals unable to give informed consent or without internet access. Patients with pituitary adenoma, individuals who are pregnant or breastfeeding, those with regular use of nasal sprays to prevent illness, allergy to hypersaline nasal sprays, or those who live in the same household as another study participant will also be excluded.
